prompt: My MapLibre GL JS stylesheet has no `glyphs` property set at all, and my symbol layers have `text-font` set to a font name. Text labels are showing up, but in a generic font, not the one I specified. Is this a bug I need to fix, or expected behavior? What's actually happening?

Description: explicit — omitted glyphs field, text renders in wrong font
prompt: My MapLibre GL JS stylesheet has no `glyphs` property set at all, and my symbol layers have `text-font` set to a font name. Text labels are showing up, but in a generic font, not the one I specified. Is this a bug I need to fix, or expected behavior? What's actually happening?
[groq-gpt-oss] evals/prompts/lib/skill-p:
### Short answer **It’s not a bug.** When a style **doesn’t have a `glyphs` URL**, MapLibre GL JS (v5.11 + and all later versions) automatically falls back to **“local-fonts mode.”** In that mode every name that appears in a layer’s `text-font` array is treated exactly like a CSS `font-family` list: 1. The browser tries to find a **system font** with that name. 2. If you have added a **web-font** (via `@font-face` or `map.setFontFaces()`), the browser will load it and use it. 3. If the name can’t be resolved, the browser picks its own generic fallback (usually *sans-serif*), which is why you see a “generic” font on the map. So the map is working as designed; the only thing missing is a **real font file that matches the name you put in `text-font`.** Below is a deeper dive into what’s happening, why you see the generic font, and how to get the exact font you want—both for GL JS and for MapLibre Native (which *does* require a `glyphs` URL). --- ## 1. What MapLibre GL JS does when `glyphs` is omitted | Step | What the engine does | Result | |------|----------------------|--------| | **a.** | Reads the `text-font` array (e.g. `["My Custom Font Bold", "Noto Sans Regular"]`). | The list is now a **fallback chain** just like CSS. | | **b.** | For each **code-point** it asks the browser’s text layout engine to rasterise the glyph using the first font that can render it. | No glyph-PBF request is ever made. | | **c.** | If the font name is **not known** to the browser (no system font, no loaded web-font), the browser falls back to its own generic family (`sans-serif`, `serif`, etc.). | You see a generic font that varies by OS / browser. | | **d.** | The rendered glyphs are turned into an **SDF texture** on-the-fly (TinySDF) and drawn on the map. | Text appears, but not in the font you expected. | > **Key point:** The `glyphs` field is *optional* in GL JS ≥ 5.11. The engine deliberately **does not treat the missing URL as an error**; it simply switches to the local-font path. ### Why the generic font appears * **The font isn’t installed on the client OS** (e.g. “My Custom Font” is a brand font you only have on your design workstation). * **You haven’t loaded the font as a web-font** (no `@font-face` rule, no `font-faces` entry, or the URL is wrong / blocked by CORS). * The name you wrote in `text-font` **doesn’t exactly match** the `font-family` name declared in the font file (case-sensitive, spaces, hyphens, etc.). When any of those happen, the browser’s own fallback chain takes over, which is why you see a “generic” sans-serif. --- ## 2. How to make the intended font actually appear You have **three common ways** to supply the font that `text-font` refers to: ### 2.1. Load a web-font with plain CSS (`@font-face`) ```css @font-face { font-family: "My Custom Font"; src: url("/fonts/MyCustomFont-Regular.woff2") format("woff2"), url("/fonts/MyCustomFont-Regular.woff") format("woff"); font-weight: normal; font-style: normal; } ``` * Put the CSS in your page (or a linked stylesheet). * Make sure the URL is reachable **from the browser** (CORS headers if it’s on another origin). * Use the exact same string in `text-font`: ```json { "type": "symbol", "layout": { "text-field": "{name}", "text-font": ["My Custom Font Regular", "Noto Sans Regular"] } } ``` **Result:** The browser loads the font, TinySDF rasterises it, and you see the exact typeface. ### 2.2. Declare the font in the style’s `font-faces` property (GL JS ≥ 6.7) ```json { "font-faces": { "My Custom Font Regular": [ { "url": "https://example.com/fonts/MyCustomFont-Regular.ttf", "unicode-range": ["U+0000-FFFF"] // optional, can limit to needed blocks } ] } } ``` * The style JSON now tells MapLibre **which file to fetch** for the given `text-font` name. * GL JS will request the file **through the browser**, so the same CORS rules apply. * You can change the mapping at runtime with `map.setFontFaces()` if you need dynamic swapping. ### 2.3. Use a system-installed font (rare for web) If the font is already installed on the user’s OS under the exact name you use in `text-font`, the browser will pick it automatically. This is the least reliable approach for public web maps because you can’t control what fonts your visitors have. --- ## 3. When you *must* serve glyph PBFs (e.g. for MapLibre Native) Native SDKs **do not have the local-font fallback**. If you want the same look on both GL JS and Native, you need a `glyphs` URL that serves **SDF glyph PBFs** for every font you reference. Typical workflow: 1. **Pick a font** that you already have PBFs for (e.g. Noto Sans from `fonts.openmaptiles.org`). 2. **Self-host** the `{fontstack}/{range}.pbf` tree (or copy the OpenMapTiles `fonts` repo). 3. Set the style’s `glyphs` field, e.g.: ```json "glyphs": "https://my.cdn.com/fonts/{fontstack}/{range}.pbf" ``` 4. Keep the same `text-font` names you used in GL JS. 5. (Optional) Add a `font-faces` entry if you also want the browser to load the TTF/OTF for complex scripts (Arabic, Devanagari, etc.) – Native will ignore it, GL JS will use it. If you only need GL JS and you’re happy with the local-font path, you can **skip step 1-4** entirely, but remember that Native will fall back to a generic system font or fail to render those labels. --- ## 4. Special script handling – why some scripts ignore `text-font` | Script | How it’s rendered in GL JS (≥ 6.7) | What you need to do | |--------|-----------------------------------|---------------------| | **CJK (Chinese, Japanese, Korean)** | Rendered **locally** by default via `localIdeographFontFamily`. `text-font` is ignored (except for weight). | Usually you *don’t* need glyph PBFs. If you want a specific on-device CJK font, set `localIdeographFontFamily` to that family name. | | **Arabic, Hebrew (RTL)** | Shaped locally in GL JS ≥ 6.9. No plugin needed. | Just list the desired Noto/Roboto font in `text-font`. | | **Devanagari, Thai, Khmer, Myanmar, etc. (complex shaping)** | Since GL JS 6.15, drawn **with the browser’s text engine** (grapheme-cluster aware). Glyph PBFs are ignored. | Declare the font file in `font-faces` (or load via CSS) so the browser can find the correct typeface. | | **Latin, Cyrillic, Greek, etc.** | Rendered from glyph PBFs *if* a `glyphs` URL exists; otherwise from local fonts. | Either serve PBFs or load the font locally. | > **Bottom line:** For any script that requires shaping (Arabic, Devanagari, etc.) you **must** provide a web-font or `font-faces` entry; the glyph server alone won’t be enough. --- ## 5. Checklist – “Why isn’t my custom font showing?” | ✅ | Item | How to verify | |----|------|----------------| | 1 | `glyphs` is **absent** (or you deliberately want local fonts). | Look at the top-level of your style JSON. | | 2 | The **font name** in `text-font` exactly matches the `font-family` declared in the font file (case-sensitive, spaces, hyphens). | Open the TTF/OTF in a font viewer or check the `name` table. | | 3 | The font file is **reachable** by the browser (CORS headers `Access-Control-Allow-Origin:*` or your domain). | Open the URL directly in a new tab; it should download without a CORS error in the console. | | 4 | The font is **actually loaded** before the map draws. | In Chrome DevTools → **Network** tab filter “font”. You should see the request and a 200 response. | | 5 | No **CSS overrides** are changing `font-family` for the map container. | Inspect the map canvas element; ensure no `font-family` style is applied that could interfere. | | 6 | If you use `font-faces`, the **style JSON** includes it and the map has been re-loaded after the change. | Check `map.getStyle().fontFaces` (or `map.getStyle().glyphs`) in the console. | | 7 | For **CJK** you haven’t unintentionally disabled `localIdeographFontFamily`. | Verify `map.getLocalIdeographFontFamily()` (or the option you passed). | | 8 | For **Native** you have a `glyphs` URL (otherwise the text will fall back to the device’s default). | Look at the native app’s style JSON; add a glyph server if needed. | If any of the above fails, the browser will fall back to its generic font, which is exactly what you’re seeing. --- ## 6. Example – Getting a brand font to work (GL JS only) ```html MapLibre – custom local font
``` *Result:* “Acme City” appears in **Acme Bold** (if the font loads). If the font fails to load, the browser falls back to **Noto Sans Regular** (or the generic sans-serif). --- ## 7. TL;DR – What you should do | Situation | Action | |-----------|--------| | **You see generic text** and **`glyphs` is missing** | Load the desired font as a web-font (`@font-face`) **or** add a `font-faces` entry that points to the TTF/OTF. Make sure the name matches exactly. | | **You want the same look on Native** | Add a proper `glyphs` URL that serves SDF PBFs for the font (or use a pre-built font set like OpenMapTiles). Keep `font-faces` for complex scripts if you need shaping. | | **You’re using CJK and don’t care about the exact shape** | Leave `glyphs` omitted; let `localIdeographFontFamily` generate the glyphs locally (fast, low network). | | **You need Arabic, Devanagari, etc.

Description: implicit — offline/local fonts on MapLibre Native, not GL JS
prompt: I'm building an offline map app with MapLibre Native on Android and want labels to render in local device fonts without running a glyphs server. What's the right way to configure this?
[groq-gpt-oss] evals/prompts/lib/skill-p:
## TL;DR MapLibre Native **cannot omit the `glyphs` field** – it will try to fetch a glyph-PBF for every `text-font` you use. What you *can* do for a fully offline Android app is: 1. **Bundle the font files you want to use** (TTF/OTF) in the APK (assets or `res/font`). 2. **Declare those fonts in the style’s `font-faces` property** so the native renderer knows which file to use for each `text-font` name (and, optionally, which Unicode ranges they cover). 3. **Provide a minimal local glyph-server stub** (or a set of empty PBF files) that satisfies the required `glyphs` URL – the renderer will fall back to the `font-faces` files for every code-point, so the stub never actually needs to contain real glyph data. That gives you true offline label rendering with the device’s fonts, without having to run a remote glyph-PBF service. Below is a step-by-step guide, plus the “gotchas” you’ll hit along the way. --- ## 1. Understand the native limitation | Platform | What happens if `glyphs` is missing? | |----------|---------------------------------------| | **MapLibre GL JS (≥ 5.11.0)** | Falls back to **local-font rendering** (TinySDF) – you can omit `glyphs` completely. | | **MapLibre Native (Android)** | **No fallback** – the style must contain a `glyphs` URL. If the request fails the whole tile is considered missing and the label disappears.
*(Issue #165 is still open.)* | So for Android you *must* give the SDK a `glyphs` URL, even if you never intend to use the PBFs. --- ## 2. Bundle the fonts you want to use ### a. Choose the fonts * For a global map the safest choice is the **Noto** family (Noto Sans, Noto Sans CJK SC/TC/JP/KR, Noto Sans Arabic, Noto Sans Devanagari, …). * If you have a brand font, just add its TTF/OTF. ### b. Add them to the APK ``` app/ └─ src/ └─ main/ ├─ assets/ │ └─ fonts/ │ ├─ NotoSans-Regular.ttf │ ├─ NotoSansArabic-Regular.ttf │ └─ NotoSansDevanagari-Regular.ttf └─ res/ └─ font/ └─ (optional) XML font-family resources ``` > **Why assets?** `font-faces` URLs are resolved by the native SDK the same way a browser would resolve a normal URL. Using the `file:///android_asset/…` scheme works out-of-the-box and does not require any extra Android-specific code. --- ## 3. Declare the fonts in the style (`font-faces`) Add a top-level `font-faces` object to your style JSON. The keys are the **exact strings you will use in `text-font`** (including weight keywords if you need them). Each entry is an array of objects that point at the bundled TTF/OTF and optionally limit the Unicode range. ```json { "version": 8, "glyphs": "file:///android_asset/glyphs/{fontstack}/{range}.pbf", "font-faces": { "Noto Sans Regular": [ { "url": "file:///android_asset/fonts/NotoSans-Regular.ttf", "unicode-range": ["U+0000-00FF", "U+0100-024F"] // Latin, Latin-Extended } ], "Noto Sans Arabic": [ { "url": "file:///android_asset/fonts/NotoSansArabic-Regular.ttf", "unicode-range": ["U+0600-06FF", "U+0750-077F"] } ], "Noto Sans Devanagari": [ { "url": "file:///android_asset/fonts/NotoSansDevanagari-Regular.ttf", "unicode-range": ["U+0900-097F"] } ], "Noto Sans CJK SC": [ { "url": "file:///android_asset/fonts/NotoSansCJKSC-Regular.otf", "unicode-range": ["U+4E00-9FFF", "U+3400-4DBF"] } ] }, "layers": [ { "id": "place-labels", "type": "symbol", "source": "osm", "source-layer": "place", "layout": { "text-field": ["get", "name"], "text-font": [ "Noto Sans Bold", "Noto Sans Regular" ], "text-size": 12 } } ] } ``` **Key points** * **Exact match** – `text-font` must contain the same string (`"Noto Sans Regular"`). * **Unicode-range** – optional but recommended; it tells the renderer which file to use for which code-points and prevents it from trying the (non-existent) glyph PBFs for those ranges. * **Weight handling** – you can add a second entry for `"Noto Sans Bold"` that points at the bold TTF/OTF, or you can rely on the `font-weight` property in the layer (the SDK will synthesize a bold style from the regular file if no bold file is supplied). --- ## 4. Satisfy the required `glyphs` URL Because Native will *always* try to download a glyph PBF, you need a URL that resolves locally and never fails. Two practical approaches: ### 4.1. Empty-file stub Create an empty folder hierarchy that matches the `{fontstack}/{range}` pattern and ship **empty `.pbf` files** (0 bytes or a minimal valid PBF header). Put it under `assets/glyphs/`: ``` assets/ └─ glyphs/ ├─ Noto%20Sans%20Regular/ │ └─ 0-255.pbf ├─ Noto%20Sans%20Arabic/ │ └─ 0-255.pbf └─ … (one empty file per font-stack you use) ``` The style’s `glyphs` field points at it: ```json "glyphs": "file:///android_asset/glyphs/{fontstack}/{range}.pbf" ``` When the SDK requests a range, it gets an empty PBF, which contains no glyphs. The renderer then falls back to the `font-faces` entry for that code-point, so the label still appears. ### 4.2. Tiny local HTTP server (optional) If you prefer a “real” glyph server (e.g., you already run a tiny Jetty/OkHttp server for other assets), expose the same path and return **HTTP 404** for any request. The native SDK treats a 404 as “glyph not found” and will still use `font-faces`. The advantage is you don’t have to ship a bunch of empty files, but you do need a small server thread. > **Which to pick?** > *Empty files* are the simplest and have zero runtime overhead. Use a local server only if you already have one for other reasons. --- ## 5. Put it all together in Android code ```kotlin // 1️⃣ Load the style JSON from assets (or from a remote source you have cached) val styleJson = assets.open("style/offline-style.json") .bufferedReader() .use { it.readText() } // 2️⃣ Create the MapLibre map val map = MapLibreMap( context = this, mapOptions = MapOptions( // No need for a remote style URL – we pass the JSON directly styleJson = styleJson, // Optional: set the initial camera, etc. ) ) // 3️⃣ Add the map view to your layout mapView = MapView(this) mapView.getMapAsync { mapLibreMap -> // Map is ready – you can now add sources, layers, etc. } ``` Because the style already contains the `glyphs` URL that points at `file:///android_asset/...`, the map works completely offline. All label rendering is performed by the bundled TTF/OTF files via the `font-faces` mapping. --- ## 6. Special script handling | Script | What you need to do in the style | |--------|----------------------------------| | **CJK (Chinese, Japanese, Korean)** | Native does **not** have the `localIdeographFontFamily` shortcut that GL JS has. If you want the on-device font you must provide a `font-faces` entry for the CJK font (as shown above). The empty glyph PBFs will be ignored for those code-points. | | **Arabic / Hebrew (RTL)** | No extra plugin is required in Native (it uses HarfBuzz). Just list the appropriate Noto-Sans-Arabic / Noto-Sans-Hebrew in `text-font`. | | **Devanagari, Thai, Khmer, Myanmar, etc.** | These scripts need proper shaping. Native will use HarfBuzz **only** when a matching `font-faces` entry exists. The `unicode-range` you set should cover the whole script block. | | **Latin + fallback** | Keep a generic `"Noto Sans Regular"` entry for the basic Latin range; you can also add a `"Noto Sans Bold"` entry if you need weight variations. | --- ## 7. Description: implicit — offline/local fonts on MapLibre Native, not GL JS
prompt: I'm building an offline map app with MapLibre Native on Android and want labels to render in local device fonts without running a glyphs server. What's the right way to configure this?
[groq-gpt-oss] evals/prompts/lib/skill-p:
Below is a **step-by-step recipe** for an Android-only MapLibre Native app that works completely offline and draws its labels from the fonts that are already on the device (or that you ship with the APK).  
The key points are:

| What you want | How you get it in MapLibre Native |
|---------------|-----------------------------------|
| **No external glyph server** | Bundle the glyph-PBF files (or a tiny “dummy” set) inside the APK and point the style’s `glyphs` URL at them with a `file:///android_asset/…` URL. |
| **Use device-installed or bundled TTF/OTF fonts** | Declare those fonts in the style’s `font-faces` property. Native reads this property at load time and uses HarfBuzz for shaping, so the actual glyph images are taken from the TTF/OTF you supplied. |
| **CJK (Chinese/Japanese/Korean) – render locally** | Native does **not** have the GL-JS `localIdeographFontFamily` shortcut, but you can avoid shipping huge CJK PBF sets by bundling a small CJK TTF/OTF (e.g. Noto Sans CJK) and referencing it in `font-faces`. The engine will rasterise the glyphs from that TTF on-device. |
| **Complex scripts (Arabic, Hebrew, Devanagari, Thai, …)** | Same as above – put the appropriate Noto-Script TTF/OTF in `font-faces`. HarfBuzz will do the shaping, so you do **not** need a glyph-PBF for those scripts. |
| **Latin / basic symbols** | You can either (a) ship the tiny Noto Sans Latin PBF set (≈ 200 KB) or (b) let the engine fall back to the TTF you listed in `font-faces`. The latter is the simplest “no-PBF” path. |

---

## 1. Prepare the assets you will ship

### a. Font files (TTF/OTF)

Download the Noto family (or any other open-source font you prefer) that covers the scripts you need:

| Script | Example file (download from Google Fonts) |
|--------|-------------------------------------------|
| Latin, Greek, Cyrillic | `NotoSans-Regular.ttf` |
| Arabic | `NotoSansArabic-Regular.ttf` |
| Hebrew | `NotoSansHebrew-Regular.ttf` |
| Devanagari | `NotoSansDevanagari-Regular.ttf` |
| Thai | `NotoSansThai-Regular.ttf` |
| CJK (Simplified Chinese) | `NotoSansCJKSC-Regular.otf` |
| CJK (Traditional Chinese) | `NotoSansCJKTC-Regular.otf` |
| CJK (Japanese) | `NotoSansCJKKR-Regular.otf` |
| … | … |

Place **all** of those files in `app/src/main/assets/fonts/` (or any sub-folder you like, just remember the path).

### b. (Optional) Minimal glyph-PBF set

If you want to keep the `glyphs` field in the style (MapLibre Native will try to load it even if you have `font-faces`), create a *tiny* set of PBFs that only contain the **basic Latin** range (U+0020-U+00FF). You can get it from the OpenMapTiles `fonts` repo or generate it yourself with **Font Maker**:

```bash
# one-off example using the Docker image that ships Font Maker
docker run --rm -v $(pwd)/fonts:/fonts \
  maplibre/font-maker \
  --font NotoSans-Regular.ttf \
  --output /fonts/NotoSans-Regular
```

Copy the resulting folder structure (`NotoSans-Regular/0-255.pbf`, `NotoSans-Regular/256-511.pbf`, …) into `app/src/main/assets/glyphs/`.

> **Why keep a tiny PBF set?**  
> The style spec requires a `glyphs` URL. If you point it at a local folder that only contains the Latin range, the engine will fetch those few files and fall back to the TTFs for everything else. This keeps the APK size low while satisfying the spec.

---

## 2. Write the **offline style JSON**

Below is a minimal style that demonstrates the three pieces you need:

```json
{
  "version": 8,
  "name": "Offline demo",
  "glyphs": "file:///android_asset/glyphs/{fontstack}/{range}.pbf",
  "font-faces": {
    "Noto Sans Regular": [
      {
        "url": "file:///android_asset/fonts/NotoSans-Regular.ttf",
        "unicode-range": ["U+0000-00FF"]               // Latin, basic punctuation
      }
    ],
    "Noto Sans Arabic": [
      {
        "url": "file:///android_asset/fonts/NotoSansArabic-Regular.ttf",
        "unicode-range": ["U+0600-06FF"]
      }
    ],
    "Noto Sans Devanagari": [
      {
        "url": "file:///android_asset/fonts/NotoSansDevanagari-Regular.ttf",
        "unicode-range": ["U+0900-097F"]
      }
    ],
    "Noto Sans CJK SC": [
      {
        "url": "file:///android_asset/fonts/NotoSansCJKSC-Regular.otf",
        "unicode-range": ["U+4E00-9FFF"]               // CJK Unified Ideographs
      }
    ]
    // …add any other script you need
  },

  "sources": {
    "osm": {
      "type": "vector",
      "url": "file:///android_asset/tiles/tileset.json"
    }
  },

  "layers": [
    {
      "id": "water",
      "type": "fill",
      "source": "osm",
      "source-layer": "water",
      "paint": { "fill-color": "#a0c8f0" }
    },
    {
      "id": "place-labels",
      "type": "symbol",
      "source": "osm",
      "source-layer": "place",
      "layout": {
        "text-field": ["get", "name"],
        "text-font": [
          "Noto Sans Regular",
          "Noto Sans Arabic",
          "Noto Sans Devanagari",
          "Noto Sans CJK SC"
        ],
        "text-size": 14,
        "text-anchor": "center"
      },
      "paint": {
        "text-color": "#222"
      }
    }
  ]
}
```

**Key things to notice**

* `glyphs` points at a **file URL** inside the APK. The `{fontstack}` placeholder will be replaced by the comma-joined list from `text-font`.  
* Every `text-font` name you use **must appear** in `font-faces`. The `unicode-range` entries tell the engine which TTF to use for which code points.  
* The style still contains a `glyphs` field because the native SDK validates the spec; the tiny Latin PBF set satisfies that requirement without pulling any network traffic.  

---

## 3. Load the style in Android

```kotlin
import org.maplibre.android.maps.MapView
import org.maplibre.android.maps.Style
import org.maplibre.android.maps.MapLibre

class OfflineMapActivity : AppCompatActivity() {

    private lateinit var mapView: MapView

    override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
        super.onCreate(savedInstanceState)

        // Initialise the MapLibre SDK (once per process)
        MapLibre.getInstance(this)

        setContentView(R.layout.activity_offline_map)
        mapView = findViewById(R.id.mapView)

        mapView.getMapAsync { mapboxMap ->
            // The style JSON lives in assets/offline-style.json
            mapboxMap.setStyle(
                Style.Builder()
                    .fromUri("asset://offline-style.json")
            ) { style ->
                // style is ready – you can add sources, layers, etc. if you want
            }
        }
    }

    override fun onStart() {
        super.onStart()
        mapView.onStart()
    }
    override fun onStop() {
        super.onStop()
        mapView.onStop()
    }
    override fun onLowMemory() {
        super.onLowMemory()
        mapView.onLowMemory()
    }
    override fun onDestroy() {
        super.onDestroy()
        mapView.onDestroy()
    }
}
```

* `asset://offline-style.json` tells the native SDK to read the file from `src/main/assets/`.  
* Because the style uses `file:///android_asset/…` URLs for both glyphs and fonts, **no network request is ever made**.  

---

## 4. What about CJK “ideographs”?

MapLibre Native **does not have** the GL-JS `localIdeographFontFamily` shortcut, so if you want CJK characters to look decent you must provide a font that contains those glyphs. The simplest approach is:

1. Ship a **single** CJK TTF/OTF (e.g. `NotoSansCJKSC-Regular.otf`).  
2. Reference it in `font-faces` as shown above.  
3. **Do not** try to generate a full CJK glyph-PBF set – it would be tens of megabytes and would defeat the offline goal.

The native engine will rasterise the glyphs from that TTF on-the-fly (Harfbuzz does the shaping, the renderer does the SDF conversion). The result is crisp at any zoom level and the APK size increase is only a few megabytes.

---

## 5. Handling right-to-left (RTL) scripts
